name: What is psychology?
q: What is psychology, and what does the field involve as a science and profession?
ans:
The scientific study of the mind and behaviour (APA)
Scientific inquiry: observation, experimentation, testing and analysis
Multiple perspectives: biological, cognitive, emotional, personal and social influences
A diverse field: cognitive, developmental, social, personality, clinical, counselling, health, educational, I/O and more
Both research and practice: address psychological difficulties, promote well-being and performance, improve human-centred technologies and systems

name: Wilhelm Wundt
q: Who was Wilhelm Wundt and why is he important to psychology?
ans:
Father of psychology
Set up the world's first psychology lab at the University of Leipzig in 1879
Believed consciousness could be broken down into thoughts, experiences, emotions and other basic elements
Used objective introspection

name: Objective introspection
q: What is objective introspection and who used it?
ans:
Wundt's method
Objectively examining and measuring one's own thoughts and mental activities

name: Structuralism
q: What is structuralism, who founded it, and what did it focus on?
ans:
Edward Titchener — Wundt's student who brought Wundt's ideas to America
Focused on the structure of the mind
Experiences could be broken down into sensations, images and affections
Died out in the early 1900s

name: Functionalism
q: What is functionalism, who founded it, and what was its influence?
ans:
William James
Focused on how the mind allows people to adapt, live, work and play
Wrote Principles of Psychology
Influenced modern educational and industrial/organisational psychology and other fields

name: Gestalt psychology
q: What is Gestalt psychology, who founded it, and what is its key idea?
ans:
Max Wertheimer
"The whole is greater than the sum of its parts"
Sensation and perception can't be understood by breaking them into smaller elements
Gestalt ideas are now part of cognitive psychology

name: Psychoanalysis
q: What is psychoanalysis, who founded it, and what were its key ideas?
ans:
Sigmund Freud
His patients had nervous disorders with no apparent physical cause
Proposed the unconscious mind
Believed repressed urges created nervous disorders
Stressed the importance of early childhood experiences
Modern psychotherapy is based on psychoanalysis

name: Behaviourism
q: What is behaviourism, who proposed it, and what were its key ideas?
ans:
Proposed by John B. Watson
Focuses on observable behaviour only — must be directly seen and measured
Based on Pavlov's work: a reflex can be conditioned (learned)
Watson believed phobias are learned

name: Little Albert
q: What was Watson's Little Albert study and what did it show?
ans:
Watson's case study
A baby was taught to fear a white rat
Used to show phobias can be learned
Would be considered cruel by today's ethical standards

name: Psychodynamic perspective
q: What is the psychodynamic perspective and who are its major theorists?
ans:
Modern version of psychoanalysis
Focuses on development of a sense of self and the motivations behind behaviour, rather than sexual motivations
Major theorists: Carl Jung, Anna Freud, Erik Erikson

name: Behavioural perspective
q: What is the behavioural perspective and what did Skinner contribute to it?
ans:
B.F. Skinner developed operant conditioning
Explains how voluntary behaviour is learned
Introduced the concept of reinforcement
Behaviourism became a major force in the 20th century

name: Humanistic perspective
q: What is the humanistic perspective, its key ideas, and its founders?
ans:
"Third force" in psychology — a reaction to both psychoanalysis and behaviourism
People have free will: the freedom to choose their own destiny
Self-actualisation: achieving one's full potential or actual self
Early founders: Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers

name: Cognitive perspective
q: What does the cognitive perspective focus on, and what are its roots? Give an example.
ans:
Focuses on memory, intelligence, perception, thought processes, problem solving, language and learning
Example: Piaget's theory of cognitive development
Includes cognitive neuroscience: physical changes in the brain and nervous system during thinking
Has roots in Gestalt psychology

name: Sociocultural perspective
q: What does the sociocultural perspective focus on, and what areas does it include?
ans:
Focuses on the relationship between social behaviour and culture
Social psychology: groups, social roles, rules of social actions and relationships
Cultural psychology: cultural norms, values and expectations
Includes cross-cultural research

name: Biopsychological perspective
q: How does the biopsychological perspective explain behaviour, and what methods does it use?
ans:
Explains human and animal behaviour through biological events in the body
E.g., genetic influences, hormones, nervous system activity
Uses animal studies and patient studies

name: Evolutionary perspective
q: What does the evolutionary perspective focus on? Give examples.
ans:
Focuses on the biological bases of universal mental characteristics all humans share
Behaviour is seen as having adaptive or survival value
E.g., why we lie, mate selection, universal fears, why we enjoy music

name: Modern perspectives overview
q: What are the seven modern perspectives in psychology, and can one explain everything?
ans:
Seven modern perspectives: psychodynamic, behavioural, humanistic, cognitive, sociocultural, biopsychological, evolutionary
No single perspective is used to explain all human behaviour and processes

name: Psychologist vs psychiatrist vs psychiatric social worker
q: How do a psychologist, a psychiatrist and a psychiatric social worker differ?
ans:
Psychologist: doctorate (Ph.D., Psy.D. or Ed.D.); works with humans or animals; must be licensed; typically doesn't prescribe
Psychiatrist: medical doctor specialising in diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders; can prescribe medication
Psychiatric social worker: trained in social work (M.S.W.), often with a professional licence (L.C.S.W.)

name: Areas of specialisation
q: What are the main areas of specialisation in psychology?
ans:
Clinical psychology
Cognitive psychology
Developmental psychology
Social psychology
Personality psychology
Biopsychology

name: Professional guidelines
q: Which professional guidelines should psychologists follow, including in Malaysia?
ans:
Refer to each country's own guidelines
E.g., American Psychological Association, British Psychological Society, Australian Psychological Society, NZ Psychological Society
Malaysia: Lembaga Kaunselor, Malaysian Society of Clinical Psychology

name: Scientific approach
q: What is the scientific approach in psychology?
ans: A system of gathering data so that bias and error in measurement are reduced

name: Critical thinking
q: What is critical thinking?
ans: Making reasoned judgments about claims

name: Four goals of psychology
q: What are the four goals of psychology and what question does each ask?
ans:
Description: what is happening?
Explanation: why is it happening?
Prediction: when will it happen again?
Control: how can it be changed?

name: Steps in the scientific approach
q: What are the five steps in the scientific approach?
ans:
1. Perceive the question
2. Form a hypothesis
3. Test the hypothesis
4. Draw conclusions
5. Report your results

name: Why research ethics?
q: Why are research ethics needed in psychology?
ans:
As psychology and research on people and animals grew, protections were needed
Studies like Little Albert would be cruel by today's standards
Ethical treatment of research participants must be ensured

name: Institutional review boards (IRBs)
q: What are institutional review boards (IRBs) and what do they do?
ans:
Groups of psychologists or other professionals
Review each proposed study and judge its safety and consideration for participants
E.g., HELP Ethics Review Board

name: Common ethical guidelines
q: What are the common ethical guidelines for research with human participants?
ans:
Weigh participants' rights and well-being against the study's value
Informed consent: participants make an informed decision
Deception must be justified
Participants may withdraw at any time
Protect participants from risks, or tell them explicitly
Investigators must debrief participants
Data must remain confidential
Researchers must detect and correct any undesirable consequences

name: Animal research
q: Why is animal research used in psychology, and what ethical rules apply?
ans:
Answers questions we could never investigate with humans
Avoid exposing animals to unnecessary pain or suffering
Only about 7% of psychological studies use animals

name: Personality
q: What is personality in psychology?
ans:
Unique and relatively stable ways people think, feel and behave
An area of psychology with several ways to explain people's characteristic behaviour

name: Levels of the mind
q: What are Freud's three levels of the mind?
ans:
Freud divided the mind into three levels:
Conscious
Preconscious
Unconscious

name: Id
q: What is the id, what are its characteristics, and what principle does it follow?
ans:
Completely unconscious
Innate — present at birth
Home to basic biological drives (hunger, self-preservation, sex)
Acts like an infant: demanding, irrational, illogical, impulsive
Runs on the pleasure principle — "if it feels good, do it"

name: Ego
q: What is the ego, what principle does it follow, and what is its role?
ans:
Mostly conscious, rational and logical
Deals with reality
Follows the reality principle
Executive director — referee between id and superego

name: Superego
q: What is the superego and how does it develop?
ans:
Moral centre of personality
Develops as children learn society's rules, customs and expectations
Contains the conscience (source of guilt)

name: Pleasure principle
q: What is the pleasure principle and which part of personality follows it?
ans:
Belongs to the id
Desire for immediate gratification of needs
No regard for consequences — "if it feels good, do it"

name: Reality principle
q: What is the reality principle and which part of personality follows it?
ans:
Belongs to the ego
Satisfy the id's demands only when no negative consequences will result
Denies the id when consequences would be painful or unpleasant

name: Conscience
q: What is the conscience in Freud's theory?
ans:
Part of the superego
Produces guilt after a wrongdoing

name: Defence mechanisms
q: What are defence mechanisms and how do they work?
ans:
Ways of dealing with anxiety
Work by unconsciously distorting one's perception of reality
Cope with anxiety from conflict between id, ego and superego

name: Denial
q: What is denial as a defence mechanism?
ans: Refusing to recognise or acknowledge a threatening situation

name: Repression
q: What is repression as a defence mechanism?
ans: Pushing threatening or conflicting events out of conscious memory

name: Rationalisation
q: What is rationalisation as a defence mechanism?
ans: Making up acceptable excuses for unacceptable behaviour or mistakes

name: Displacement
q: What is displacement as a defence mechanism?
ans:
Redirecting emotions (e.g., anger) onto a target
…that is not the original cause of the emotion

name: Sublimation
q: What is sublimation as a defence mechanism?
ans:
Turning socially unacceptable urges
…into socially acceptable behaviour

name: Psychosexual stages
q: What are Freud's psychosexual stages and how does fixation occur?
ans:
Freud: personality develops through a series of stages
Each stage focuses on an erogenous zone (body area that gives pleasure)
Each zone can become a source of conflict
Unresolved conflict → fixation ("stuck" at that stage)
Fixation carries emotional baggage into adulthood

name: Oral stage
q: What happens in Freud's oral stage: age, zone, conflict and fixation?
ans:
Age: first 18 months
Erogenous zone: mouth
Conflict: weaning
Fixation: overeating, chain smoking, nail biting

name: Anal stage
q: What happens in Freud's anal stage: age, zone, conflict and fixation?
ans:
Age: 18–36 months
Erogenous zone: anus (holding and releasing faeces)
Conflict: toilet training
Fixation: anal expulsive or anal retentive personality

name: Phallic stage
q: What happens in Freud's phallic stage: age, zone, conflict and fixation?
ans:
Age: 3–6 years
Erogenous zone: genitals
Conflict: awakening of sexual feelings
Oedipus complex / Electra complex
Fixation: promiscuous sexual behaviour

name: Latency stage
q: What happens during Freud's latency stage, and at what age?
ans:
Age: 6 years to puberty
Sexual feelings are repressed
Child develops intellectually, physically and socially
Sees the opposite sex as "awful"

name: Genital stage
q: What happens during Freud's genital stage, and when does it begin?
ans:
Age: puberty onward
Sexual feelings can no longer be ignored
Attraction focuses on others
Entry into adult social and sexual behaviour

name: Criticisms of psychodynamic theory
q: What are the main criticisms of Freud's psychodynamic theory?
ans:
Not scientific — Freud did no experiments; based only on observing his patients
Too ambiguous — relies on dream interpretation and free association; hard to falsify
Limited sample — wealthy Austrian women in the Victorian era, when sexual repression was common

name: Behavioural view of personality
q: How does the behavioural view explain personality? Give an example.
ans:
Personality = a set of learned responses
Learned through classical and operant conditioning
Skinner: mental processes can't sufficiently explain behaviour
E.g., shyness explained by operant conditioning

name: Social cognitive view
q: How does the social cognitive view explain personality and behaviour?
ans:
Learning is shaped by other people's behaviour
…and by one's own expectancies
Behaviour governed by external stimuli AND cognitive processes
E.g., observational learning

name: Reciprocal determinism
q: What is Bandura's reciprocal determinism and what factors does it involve?
ans:
Bandura
Three factors: environment, behaviour, personal/cognitive factors
Each influences the others (give-and-take)

name: Self-efficacy
q: What is Bandura's concept of self-efficacy and what does it depend on?
ans:
Bandura
Expectancy of how effective one's efforts to reach a goal will be
Depends on past experience
…and perceived competence (from self and others)

name: Rotter's social learning theory
q: How does Rotter's social learning theory define personality, and what shapes it?
ans:
Personality = a relatively stable set of potential responses to situations
Shaped by two factors: expectancy and reinforcement value

name: Expectancy
q: What is expectancy in Rotter's social learning theory?
ans:
Rotter
Belief that a reinforcing consequence will follow a particular behaviour

name: Reinforcement value
q: What is reinforcement value in Rotter's theory?
ans:
Rotter
Preference for one particular reinforcer over others

name: Locus of control
q: What is Rotter's locus of control, and what are its two types?
ans:
Rotter
Whether we believe we have control over events in our lives
Internal: outcomes come from own actions
External: outcomes come from fate or other people

name: Review: behavioural & social cognitive
q: What are the criticisms and contributions of the behavioural and social cognitive views?
ans:
Criticism: behaviourists ignore mental processes
Criticism: overgeneralisation can lead to errors
Contribution: effective therapies

name: Humanistic perspective
q: What does the humanistic perspective on personality focus on, and who founded it?
ans:
Maslow and Rogers
Focuses on what makes people uniquely human
E.g., subjective feelings, freedom of choice

name: Self-concept
q: What is self-concept in humanistic theory and how does it develop?
ans:
Image of oneself
Develops from interactions with significant people
Important tool for self-actualisation

name: Self-actualisation
q: What is self-actualisation?
ans:
Striving for fulfilment
Reaching one's full potential

name: Real self vs ideal self
q: How do the real self and ideal self differ, and why does their match matter?
ans:
Real self: actual perception of own traits and abilities
Ideal self: what one should be or would like to be
Close match → competent and capable
Mismatch → anxiety and neurotic behaviour

name: Unconditional positive regard
q: What is unconditional positive regard and why is it important?
ans:
Love, affection and respect with no strings attached
Needed to explore one's full potential

name: Conditional positive regard
q: What is conditional positive regard?
ans: Positive regard given only when the provider's expectations are met

name: Fully functioning person
q: What is Rogers' fully functioning person?
ans:
In touch with and trusts their innermost urges and feelings
Real self matches ideal self
Requires unconditional positive regard

name: Review: humanistic
q: What are the criticisms and contributions of the humanistic perspective?
ans:
Criticism: idealistic
Criticism: difficult to test
Criticism: more philosophical than psychological
Contribution: therapies for self-growth and self-understanding
Contribution: shares concepts with positive psychology

name: Trait theories
q: What do trait theories of personality aim to do, and what don't they cover?
ans:
Aim to describe personality
Aim to predict future behaviour
Not about the roots or development of personality

name: Trait
q: What is a trait in personality psychology?
ans: A consistent, enduring way of thinking, feeling or behaving

name: Allport & Odbert
q: What did Allport and Odbert contribute to trait theory?
ans:
Earliest list of traits
~200 trait words from the dictionary
Believed (without evidence) traits are wired into the nervous system
Later, some evidence for heritability of traits was found

name: Surface traits
q: What are Cattell's surface traits? Give an example.
ans:
Cattell
Characteristics easily seen by others
E.g., shyness, quietness

name: Source traits
q: What are Cattell's source traits? Give an example.
ans:
Cattell
Basic traits underlying surface traits
Form the core of personality
E.g., introversion → shyness, quietness, disliking crowds

name: 16PF Questionnaire
q: What is Cattell's 16PF Questionnaire and how are its traits structured?
ans:
Cattell's Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire
Measures 16 source traits
Each trait is a dimension with two opposite ends

name: The Big Five
q: What is the Big Five model and what are its five traits?
ans:
Also called the five-factor model
OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism
Traits are independent of each other
Openness linked with better cognition and intellect

name: Trait-situation interaction
q: What is trait-situation interaction? Give an example.
ans:
The situation influences how a trait is expressed
E.g., an extravert jokes at a party but not at a funeral

name: Big Five across cultures
q: How well does the Big Five hold up across cultures?
ans:
Largely consistent across all primary cultural regions
Consistent across languages
Self-ratings match observer ratings
Regional variations still exist

name: Behavioural genetics
q: What is behavioural genetics and what evidence does it use?
ans:
Field studying the genetic bases of personality
Evidence: animal breeding — similar breeds share temperament
Evidence: twin and adoption studies

name: Twin and adoption studies (personality)
q: What have twin and adoption studies shown about personality?
ans:
Genes account for much of personality development
…regardless of shared or non-shared environment
Suggested for shyness and aggressiveness

name: The "Jim" twins
q: What did the case of the "Jim" twins show? Describe their similarities.
ans:
James Springer & James Lewis — identical twins separated at birth
Studied at age 39 (1990)
Both liked mechanical drawing and carpentry
Drank and smoked similar amounts
Both divorced a Linda and married a Betty
Both raised in Ohio by parents of similar socioeconomic background

name: Phrenology
q: What was phrenology and who proposed it?
ans:
Dr Franz Joseph Gall (1796)
Personality read from the shape of the skull
Skull bulge = brain area for a dominant personality aspect

name: DeYoung et al. (2010)
q: What did DeYoung et al. (2010) find about brain structure and Big Five traits?
ans:
MRI measured brain-area volume + Big Five questionnaire
Extraversion → higher volume in reward-value area (medial orbitofrontal cortex)
Neuroticism → lower volume in threat/punishment/negative-emotion areas (dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, posterior hippocampus)
Neuroticism → higher volume in error-detection and pain area (middle cingulate cortex)

name: Heritability
q: What is heritability, and how heritable is personality?
ans:
How much a trait in a population is due to genetics
Big Five: ~50% heritable across cultures
Personality variation: ~30–50% inherited
Environment accounts for about half

name: Individualism vs collectivism
q: How do individualistic and collectivistic cultures differ in Hofstede's model?
ans:
Hofstede
Individualistic: autonomy, change, youth, individual security, equality
Collectivistic: duty, order, tradition, respect for elders, group security, group status and hierarchy

name: Power distance
q: What is power distance in Hofstede's cultural dimensions?
ans:
Hofstede
How much less powerful members accept and expect
…that power is held by a few rather than shared equally

name: Masculinity vs femininity
q: How do masculine and feminine cultures differ in Hofstede's model?
ans:
Hofstede
"Masculine" cultures: assertive, competitive (more so for men)
"Feminine" cultures: modest, caring (for men and women)

name: Uncertainty avoidance
q: What is uncertainty avoidance, and how do low- and high-tolerance cultures differ?
ans:
Hofstede
How tolerant a culture is of uncertainty, ambiguity, unstructured situations
Less tolerant: strict rules, many safety measures, belief in One Truth
More tolerant: open to different opinions, fewer rules, religions coexist, less anxious

name: Eclectic view of assessment
q: What is the eclectic view of personality assessment, and how does purpose vary?
ans:
Professionals pick parts of different theories to fit the situation
Purpose depends on context
Researcher → classify participants by traits
Clinical/counselling psychologist → diagnose personality disorders

name: Four types of personality assessment
q: What are the four types of personality assessment? Give examples of each.
ans:
Interviews
Behavioural assessments — observation, rating scales, frequency counts
Personality inventories — 16PF, NEO-PI-3, MBTI, MMPI, etc.
Projective tests — Rorschach, TAT

name: Interviews
q: How are interviews used in personality assessment, and what are their limitations?
ans:
Professional asks questions; client answers
Focus on specific thoughts and behaviours
Unstructured (flows naturally) or semi-structured (set questions + follow-ups)
Self-report method
Limitations: halo/horn effect, questionable validity, interviewer bias

name: Behavioural assessments
q: What methods do behavioural assessments use, and what are their limitations?
ans:
Direct observation — everyday behaviour in clinical or natural setting
Rating scale — number assigned to a behaviour
Frequency count — how often a behaviour occurs in a set time
Limitations: observer effect, observer bias, no control over environment

name: Personality inventories
q: What are personality inventories and how do they work?
ans:
Commonly used by trait theorists
Questionnaire with a standard list of statements
Standardised answers (yes/no, true/false)
Paper or computer
Form of self-report

name: MMPI-3
q: What is the MMPI-3, what does it measure, and how is it used?
ans:
Tests abnormal behaviour and thinking in personality and psychopathology
335 statements
Validity scales (e.g., over-/under-reporting) + clinical and problem scales
Also used for vocational guidance and job screening

name: NEO-PI-3
q: What is the NEO-PI-3 and what does it measure?
ans:
NEO = Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness
Detailed assessment of the five main personality dimensions (OCEAN)
240 items

name: Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)
q: What is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) and what are its limitations?
ans:
Based on Carl Jung's ideas
Four dimensions: S/N, T/F, I/E, P/J
16 possible personality types
Often used for career guidance
Limited validity and reliability

name: Inventories: pros and cons
q: What are the pros and cons of personality inventories?
ans:
Pro: standardised, more objective
Pro: computer scoring free of bias
Pro: much better validity and reliability
Con: people may give socially acceptable answers
Con: questions interpreted differently
Con: individual differences in answering

name: Projective tests
q: What are projective tests and how do they work?
ans:
Show ambiguous visual stimuli
Client responds with whatever comes to mind

name: Rorschach inkblots
q: What is the Rorschach inkblot test, and how is it scored and used?
ans:
Hermann Rorschach, Swiss psychiatrist
10 inkblots — say what each looks like
Scored on colour, shape, figures seen, whole vs details
Used to describe personality, diagnose disorders, predict behaviour

name: Thematic Apperception Test (TAT)
q: What is the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) and how does it work?
ans:
Henry Murray and colleagues
20 ambiguous pictures
Client tells a story about the people in each
Psychoanalysts look for revealing statements and projection of problems

name: Projective tests: limitations
q: What are the limitations of projective tests?
ans:
Very subjective
Poor reliability and validity
No standard grading scales
Responses vary with context
Latest versions still used

name: Motivation
q: What is motivation, and how do starting, directing and continuing behaviour illustrate it?
ans:
Process by which activities are started, directed and continued
…to meet physical or psychological needs or wants
What "moves" people to act
E.g., hungry → get up (started) → go to kitchen (directed) → find food (continued)

name: Extrinsic motivation
q: What is extrinsic motivation?
ans:
Acting because it leads to an outcome
…that is separate from or external to the person

name: Intrinsic motivation
q: What is intrinsic motivation?
ans:
Acting because the act itself is rewarding
Satisfying in an internal way

name: Instinct approach
q: What does the instinct approach to motivation claim, with examples and its main criticism?
ans:
Instincts = biologically determined, innate behaviour patterns (people & animals)
Early theory: people are governed by instincts
E.g., curiosity, flight, acquisition, aggression (McDougall, 1908)
Con: doesn't explain why instincts exist
Pro: showed some behaviour is hereditary

name: Drive-reduction theory
q: What does drive-reduction theory say about where behaviour comes from and its goal?
ans:
Behaviour comes from internal drives
Drives push us to satisfy physiological needs
Goal: reduce tension and arousal

name: Need vs drive
q: How does a need differ from a drive in drive-reduction theory?
ans:
Need: requirement of some material essential for survival
Drive: tension and arousal caused by a need
Drive motivates action to fulfil the need and reduce tension

name: Primary vs acquired drives
q: How do primary drives differ from acquired drives, with examples?
ans:
Primary: body's survival needs (hunger, thirst)
Acquired (secondary): learned through experience or conditioning
E.g., need for money or social approval

name: Homeostasis
q: What is homeostasis, and what are the limits of drive-reduction theory?
ans:
Body's tendency to maintain a steady state
Limit of drive reduction: why eat when not hungry?
Limit: why do some people seek more arousal?

name: McClelland's theory
q: What are the three needs in McClelland's theory of motivation?
ans:
nAff — need for affiliation: friendly relationships
nPow — need for power: control or influence over others
nAch — need for achievement: succeed at goals, including challenging ones

name: Dweck's self-theory of motivation
q: What does Dweck's self-theory say about achievement motivation and locus of control?
ans:
Need for achievement linked to how we view ourselves
Related to locus of control
Low achievement motivation → external locus, intelligence is fixed
High achievement motivation → internal locus, intelligence is changeable

name: Arousal theory
q: What does arousal theory say about motivation and sensation seekers?
ans:
People have an optimal level of tension
Maintain it by increasing or decreasing stimulation
Sensation seekers need more arousal
E.g., free-solo climber Honnold's amygdala responded less to fear images

name: Yerkes-Dodson law
q: What does the Yerkes-Dodson law say about arousal, performance and task difficulty?
ans:
Moderate arousal → best performance
Too low or too high → worse
Easy tasks: high-moderate arousal
Difficult tasks: low-moderate arousal

name: Incentive approaches
q: What do incentive approaches say about motivation, and what is the modern push-pull view?
ans:
Behaviour = response to an external stimulus and its rewards
Incentives attract or lure people into action
Work independently of need or arousal
Modern view: "push" of internal drives + "pull" of external rewards

name: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
q: How is Maslow's hierarchy of needs structured, and what are peak experiences?
ans:
Levels of needs: deficiency needs and growth needs
Must be met before reaching self-actualisation
Peak experiences: moments when self-actualisation is temporarily achieved

name: Self-determination theory
q: What are the three needs in Ryan and Deci's self-determination theory?
ans:
Ryan & Deci (2000)
Social context affects the type of motivation
Autonomy: control over own behaviour and goals
Competence: mastering challenging tasks
Relatedness: belonging, intimacy, security with others
Supportive environment → psychological growth + more intrinsic motivation

name: Insulin and glucagon
q: What are insulin and glucagon, and how does each affect blood glucose?
ans:
Hormones from the pancreas
Control fats, proteins and carbohydrates (glucose) in the blood
Insulin ↓ blood glucose
Glucagon ↑ blood glucose

name: Leptin
q: What does the hormone leptin do in hunger regulation?
ans:
Hormone that signals the hypothalamus: "enough food"
Reduces appetite
Increases feeling of fullness

name: Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH)
q: What role does the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) play in eating, and what happens if damaged?
ans:
May stop eating when glucose levels rise
Damage → overeating

name: Lateral hypothalamus (LH)
q: What role does the lateral hypothalamus (LH) play in eating, and what happens if damaged?
ans:
Influences the start of eating when insulin rises
Damage → stops eating unless force-fed

name: Weight set point
q: What is the weight set point, and what factors affect it?
ans:
Weight level the body tries to maintain
Hypothalamus damage → drastic weight loss or gain
Metabolism matters: high metabolism → harder to gain weight
Exercise matters: offsets increases in set point

name: Basal metabolic rate (BMR)
q: What is basal metabolic rate (BMR)?
ans: Rate the body burns energy at rest

name: Social components of hunger
q: What are the social components of hunger?
ans:
Social cues and conventions
Food preferences
Culture and gender
Food as comfort or escape
Anticipating food can trigger an insulin response

name: Obesity
q: How is obesity defined, and what factors contribute to it?
ans:
Weight ≥ 20% over ideal for height
WHO (2021): BMI ≥ 25 overweight, ≥ 30 obese

name: Emotion

The "feeling" aspect of consciousness

name: Universal facial expressions

name: Labelling emotion

Cognitive element
Learned response
Shaped by language and culture

name: Sympathetic arousal in emotion

Sympathetic nervous system creates arousal

Sadness, anger, fear → higher heart rate than disgust
Anger differs from fear on vascular measures

name: Amygdala

Linked to fear and pleasure
Identifies facial expressions
Complex structure with many nuclei
Studied mainly through fear conditioning

name: Low road vs high road

Two routes from stimulus to amygdala

High road: slower, cortical — recognise threat, take conscious control

name: Other brain areas in emotion

name: Common sense theory

ans: Stimulus → emotion → physical reaction → behaviour

name: James-Lange theory
q: What does the James-Lange theory say about the order of emotion and arousal?
ans:
William James & Carl Lange
Stimulus → bodily arousal first
→ arousal interpreted and labelled as emotion

name: Evidence against James-Lange

Paralysed people still feel emotions as strongly as before

name: Cannon-Bard theory
q: What does the Cannon-Bard theory of emotion propose, and what role does the thalamus play?

Walter Cannon & Philip Bard
Physiological reaction and emotion happen at the same time
Thalamus sends signals to cortex and sympathetic NS simultaneously
Cannon: bodily changes aren't distinct enough to tell emotions apart
Criticism: vagus nerve sends feedback to the brain

name: Facial feedback hypothesis
q: What does the facial feedback hypothesis claim, and what study supports it?
ans:
Facial expressions send feedback to the brain
Feedback causes and intensifies the emotion
"The more you smile, the happier you are"
Strack et al. (1988)

name: Cognitive arousal theory
q: What does Schachter and Singer's cognitive arousal (two-factor) theory say is needed for emotion?
ans:
Schachter & Singer — two-factor theory
Need BOTH physical arousal
…AND labelling that arousal using environmental cues
→ then the emotion is experienced

name: Cognitive-mediational theory
q: What does Lazarus's cognitive-mediational theory say about the sequence of emotion?
ans:
Lazarus
Stimulus must be appraised (interpreted) first
Appraisal → emotion → bodily response
Appraisal mediates between stimulus and emotion

name: Intelligence
q: How is intelligence defined?
ans:
Ability to learn from experience
Acquire knowledge
Use resources effectively to adapt or solve problems

name: Spearman's g factor
q: What does Spearman's g factor theory propose, and what is its criticism?
ans:
g factor: general intelligence — reason, solve problems
s factor: specific intelligence — excel in certain areas
Being superior in one predicts superiority overall
Criticism: oversimplifies intelligence

name: Gardner's multiple intelligences
q: What does Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences claim, and how has it been criticised?
ans:
Howard Gardner
Nine kinds of intelligence (originally seven)
Reason, logic and knowledge are different aspects
Criticism: little or no evidence
Criticism: these are abilities, not intelligence (Hunt, 2001)

name: Sternberg's triarchic theory
q: What are the three intelligences in Sternberg's triarchic theory?
ans:
Three intelligences
Analytical: break problems into parts
Creative: handle new concepts, find new solutions
Practical: use information to get along and succeed

name: Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory
q: How did Cattell, Horn and Carroll each contribute to CHC theory?
ans:
Cattell: crystallised + fluid intelligence
Horn (Cattell's student): added other abilities

name: Crystallised vs fluid intelligence
q: How does crystallised intelligence differ from fluid intelligence?
ans:
Crystallised: acquired knowledge and skills
Fluid: problem solving and adapting in unfamiliar situations

name: Parieto-Frontal Integration Theory (P-FIT)
q: Which brain areas does the Parieto-Frontal Integration Theory (P-FIT) link to intelligence?
ans:
Frontal and parietal areas key to intelligence
Also: posterior cingulate, insular cortex, some subcortical areas
Working memory linked to fluid intelligence

name: Binet's mental ability test
q: Who developed Binet's mental ability test, why, and how did it distinguish learners?
ans:
Alfred Binet & Théodore Simon
Requested by the French education ministry
Identify children needing remedial education
Fast learners answer like older children; slow learners like younger ones

name: Mental age
q: What is mental age?
ans: Average age at which children can answer a particular level of question

name: Stanford-Binet and IQ

Lewis Terman revised Binet's test
Used William Stern's method
IQ = mental age ÷ chronological age × 100
Allowed comparison up to about age 16
Today: age-group norms instead (Stanford-Binet 5th ed.)

name: Wechsler tests
q: What are the Wechsler tests, and what scores do they produce?
ans:
David Wechsler
WAIS (adults), WISC (children), WPPSI (preschool)
Verbal + non-verbal items
Overall score + 5 index scores
Verbal comprehension, working memory, visual spatial, processing speed, fluid reasoning

name: Reliability

Test gives the same scores each time
…when given to the same people

name: Validity
q: What is validity in intelligence testing?
ans: Test measures what it's supposed to measure

name: Standardisation and norms

ans:
Give the test to a large representative group
Their scores = norms
Most tests follow a normal curve

name: Deviation IQ

ans:
IQ normally distributed
Mean 100, SD about 15
130 = two SDs above mean
70 = two SDs below mean

IQ tests reflect the test designer's culture
Language, dialect and content
Fix: culture-fair tests using non-verbal abilities

name: Usefulness of IQ tests

ans:
Predict academic success and job performance
Used in neuropsychology
Assess head injuries, learning disabilities, neuropsychological disorders

name: Intellectual disability

Also called intellectual developmental disorder
IQ below 70
Severely deficient adaptive behaviour for one's age
Affects conceptual, social, practical domains
Begins in the developmental period
Mild to profound

name: Causes of intellectual disability

Deprived environments
Chromosome/genetic disorders (e.g., Down syndrome)
Alcohol (e.g., fetal alcohol syndrome)
Dietary deficiencies
Environmental toxins

name: Giftedness
q: How is giftedness defined, and what did Terman's study find and how was it criticised?
ans:
~2% of people
IQ 130 and above
Terman's longitudinal study: most became successful adults

name: Emotional intelligence

ans:
Aware of and manage own emotions to think and reach goals
Understand what others feel
Higher EI → correlates with general intelligence
→ better relationships, seen more positively
→ better academic/job performance, greater well-being

name: Twin and adoption studies (IQ)

IQ correlation rises with genetic relatedness
Heritability of IQ ≈ 0.50 (50%)

name: Flynn effect

IQ scores steadily rising over time
In modernised countries

name: The Bell Curve & stereotype threat
