Stereotype threat: knowing a negative stereotype
…can make a person score poorly on IQ tests

name: Memory
q: How is memory defined as an active system?
ans:
An active system that receives information from the senses
Organises and alters it as it stores it away
Then retrieves it from storage

name: Three processes of memory
q: What are the three processes of memory?
ans:
Encoding: mental operations that convert sensory information into a form usable in the brain's storage systems
Storage: holding onto information for a certain duration
Retrieval: getting information out of storage

name: Information-processing model
q: What does the information-processing model of memory propose, and what are its stages?
ans:
Memory processing works like the way a computer handles information
Through three different stages (systems): sensory, short-term, long-term

name: Parallel distributed processing (PDP) model
q: What does the parallel distributed processing (PDP) model say about memory?
ans:
Memory processes take place at the same time
Over a large network of neural connections

name: Levels-of-processing model
q: What does the levels-of-processing model say, and what are its levels of processing?
ans:
Information processed more deeply (by its meaning) is remembered better and longer
Than information processed only by its sound or physical characteristics
Shallow: visual (how many vowels?) → phonemic (rhymes with?) → deep: semantic (is it used to write?)

name: Sensory memory
q: What is sensory memory, and what types does it include?
ans:
The first stage of memory
Where information enters the nervous system through the senses
Raw sensory information held for a very brief time
Includes iconic (visual) and echoic (auditory) memory

name: Iconic memory
q: How does iconic memory differ in capacity and duration?
ans:
Visual sensory memory
Capacity: everything that can be seen at one time
Duration: about a quarter of a second
New information quickly pushes it out (masking)

name: Sperling's test & eidetic imagery
q: What did Sperling's experiment show about iconic memory, and what is eidetic imagery?
ans:
Sperling: a grid of letters, then a tone signalled which row to recall
Participants could recall the cued row, so the whole grid was in iconic memory
The longer the delay before the tone, the fewer letters recalled
Eidetic imagery: rare ability to access iconic memory over a long time

name: Echoic memory
q: What is echoic memory, and how do its capacity and duration compare with iconic memory?
ans:
Brief memory of something just heard
Capacity: what can be heard at one moment (smaller than iconic)
Duration: longer than iconic, about 2 to 4 seconds

name: Selective attention
q: What is selective attention, and how do Broadbent's and Treisman's models explain it?
ans:
Ability to focus on only one stimulus from all sensory input
Broadbent's filter model: bottleneck between sensory memory and STM
Treisman's attenuation model: unselected stimuli are weakened (attenuated), not fully blocked

name: Short-term memory (STM)
q: What is short-term memory, and what are its duration and vulnerabilities?
ans:
Second stage: information held briefly while being used (also called working memory)
Duration: 12 to 30 seconds without rehearsal
Easily disrupted by interference (e.g. interrupted counting means starting over)
Tends to be encoded in auditory form

name: Maintenance rehearsal
q: What is maintenance rehearsal?
ans:
Repeating bits of information in one's head
To keep them in short-term memory

name: STM capacity & chunking
q: What is the capacity of short-term memory, and how does chunking help?
ans:
Capacity: about 5 to 9 items (Miller's magic number 7 ± 2)
Digit-span test: recall a series of numbers in order
Chunking: combine bits into meaningful units so more fits in STM

name: Working memory model
q: What does Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model propose, and what are its components?
ans:
Baddeley & Hitch (1974): an updated concept of STM
Working memory is an active system that processes information in STM
Slave systems: phonological loop, visuo-spatial sketchpad, episodic buffer
Controlled by the central executive

name: Long-term memory (LTM)
q: What is long-term memory, and how permanent is it?
ans:
The final stage of memory
Information kept more or less permanently
Not entirely infinite: meaningful and important memories are stored longer

name: Rote learning vs elaborative rehearsal
q: How does rote learning differ from elaborative rehearsal in moving information into LTM?
ans:
Two ways to move information from STM into LTM
Rote learning: repeating it over and over (maintenance rehearsal)
Elaborative rehearsal: making it meaningful, which adds retrieval cues
Elaborative rehearsal links to the levels-of-processing model

name: Nondeclarative (implicit) memory
q: What is nondeclarative (implicit) memory, and what does it include?
ans:
LTM for skills, procedures, habits and conditioned responses
Not conscious, but shows in behaviour
Includes emotional associations and simple conditioned reflexes

name: Declarative (explicit) memory
q: What is declarative (explicit) memory, and what are its two types?
ans:
LTM containing conscious, known information
E.g. factual knowledge, memories of personal events
Two types: semantic and episodic

name: Semantic memory
q: What is semantic memory?
ans:
Declarative memory for general knowledge
Language, concepts and terms, often learned in formal education

name: Episodic memory
q: What is episodic memory?
ans:
Declarative memory for personal information not available to others
Daily activities and events (e.g. what you had for breakfast)

name: Semantic network model
q: How does the semantic network model say long-term memory is organised?
ans:
LTM is organised by related meanings and concepts
Information is stored in a connected way
Related concepts are stored physically closer together

name: Retrieval cue
q: What is a retrieval cue, and why do retrieval problems occur?
ans:
A stimulus for remembering
The more retrieval cues stored with information, the easier it is to retrieve
Retrieval problems often come from how information was put into LTM

name: Encoding specificity
q: What is encoding specificity, and how do context-dependent and state-dependent learning differ?
ans:
Memory improves when information available at encoding is also there at retrieval
Context-dependent: the physical place you learned in acts as a retrieval cue
State-dependent: easier recall in a similar physiological or psychological state

name: Recall vs recognition
q: How does recall differ from recognition, including their typical errors?
ans:
Recall: pulling information out with very few external cues
Retrieval failure, e.g. tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) phenomenon
Recognition: matching information to a stored image or fact
False positive: thinking you recognise something not actually in memory

name: Serial position effect
q: What is the serial position effect, and what are the primacy and recency effects?
ans:
Information at the beginning and end of a list is remembered better than the middle
Primacy effect: better memory for the beginning
Recency effect: better memory for the end

name: Automatic encoding & flashbulb memories
q: What is automatic encoding, and what are flashbulb memories?
ans:
Automatic encoding: some information enters LTM with little or no effortful encoding
Flashbulb memory: automatic encoding of an unexpected event with strong emotional associations

name: Constructive processing
q: What does constructive processing say about how memories are retrieved?
ans:
Memories are built, or reconstructed, from information stored during encoding
Each retrieval can alter, revise or be influenced by newer information

name: Hindsight bias
q: What is hindsight bias, and why does it happen?
ans:
Falsely believing you could have predicted an event's outcome
Because older memories are revised to include newer information

name: Misinformation effect & false memory syndrome
q: What are the misinformation effect and false memory syndrome?
ans:
Misinformation effect: misleading information after an event alters the memory of it
False memory syndrome: false memories created through others' suggestion, often under hypnosis
False memories can't be created for just anything; they must be plausible

name: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve
q: What does Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve show about the rate of forgetting?
ans:
Forgetting is very fast in the first hour after learning
Then it tapers off gradually

name: Massed vs distributed practice
q: How does massed practice differ from distributed practice, and which works better?
ans:
Massed practice: studying everything at once (cramming)
Distributed practice: spacing study sessions out
Distributed practice gives better retrieval

name: Encoding failure
q: What is encoding failure as an explanation of forgetting, with an example?
ans:
Forgetting because the information was never processed into memory
E.g. you can't name the last 5 vehicles you passed on the way to class

name: Memory trace decay theory
q: What does memory trace decay theory say about forgetting, and what is its limitation?
ans:
Memory trace: physical change in the brain when a memory forms
Decay: memory lost over time when the trace isn't used (sensory memory, STM)
Disuse: unused LTM memories eventually decay
Can't explain memories recalled after many years

name: Proactive vs retroactive interference
q: How does proactive interference differ from retroactive interference?
ans:
Proactive interference: older information interferes with retrieving newer information
Retroactive interference: newer information interferes with retrieving older information

name: Brain areas for memory
q: Which brain areas are involved in the different types of memory?
ans:
Motor cortex and cerebellum: procedural memories
Prefrontal cortex: STM
Frontal and temporal lobes: semantic and episodic memories
Hippocampus: forming new semantic and episodic memories
Amygdala: new emotional memories
Posterior parietal cortex: episodic memory retrieval

name: Consolidation & long-term potentiation
q: What are consolidation and long-term potentiation in memory formation?
ans:
Consolidation: changes in neuron structure and function when a memory forms
Long-term potentiation: more, and more sensitive, receptor sites/synapses through repeated stimulation
Hippocampus: forms new long-term declarative memories

name: Patient H.M.
q: What happened to patient H.M., and what did his case show about memory?
ans:
Had severe epileptic seizures
Hippocampi and nearby medial temporal lobe structures were removed
Could not form new declarative (semantic and episodic) memories
Nondeclarative memory stayed intact
Shows the hippocampus consolidates and stores new information

name: Retrograde vs anterograde amnesia
q: How does retrograde amnesia differ from anterograde amnesia?
ans:
Retrograde: loss of memory from the injury or trauma backwards (the past)
Anterograde: loss from the injury forwards; can't form new long-term memories

name: Alzheimer's disease
q: What is Alzheimer's disease, how does its amnesia progress, and what are its risk factors?
ans:
Most common type of dementia in the elderly
Mainly anterograde amnesia at first; retrograde amnesia later
Drugs can slow it, but not stop or reverse it
Risk factors: high cholesterol, high blood pressure, smoking, obesity, type II diabetes, lack of exercise

name: Infantile amnesia
q: What is infantile amnesia, and why can't we recall early memories?
ans:
Inability to retrieve memories from before age three
Earliest memories may be implicit and hard to report
Explicit memory develops with hippocampus changes and language skills
Explicit memory gives rise to autobiographical memory

name: Learning
q: What is learning, and how does it differ from maturation?
ans:
Any relatively permanent change in behaviour
Brought about by experience or practice
Part of the brain is physically changed to record what was learned
Not all change is learning: some is maturation (e.g. learning to walk)

name: Ivan Pavlov
q: Who was Ivan Pavlov and what did he discover?
ans:
Russian physiologist
Discovered classical conditioning through his work on digestion in dogs

name: Classical conditioning
q: What is classical conditioning?
clues: stimulus other than the natural one
ans:
Learning to make an involuntary response
To a stimulus other than the original, natural stimulus that normally produces the response

name: Reflex
q: What is a reflex?
ans: An unlearned, involuntary response

name: Neutral stimulus (NS)
q: What is a neutral stimulus (NS) in classical conditioning? Give an example.
ans:
A stimulus that produces no reflex response at first
E.g. the metronome before conditioning: no salivation
Can become a conditioned stimulus when paired with the UCS

name: Unconditioned stimulus (UCS)
q: What is an unconditioned stimulus (UCS)? Give an example.
ans:
A naturally occurring stimulus
Leads to an involuntary and unlearned response
E.g. food

name: Unconditioned response (UCR)
q: What is an unconditioned response (UCR)? Give an example.
ans:
An involuntary and unlearned response
To a naturally occurring (unconditioned) stimulus
E.g. salivation to food

name: Conditioned stimulus (CS)
q: What is a conditioned stimulus (CS), and how does it become one?
ans:
Stimulus that produces a learned response
Because it has been paired with the original unconditioned stimulus
A neutral stimulus becomes the CS after pairing

name: Conditioned response (CR)
q: What is a conditioned response (CR)? Give an example.
ans:
Learned, reflex-like response to a conditioned stimulus
Sometimes called a conditioned reflex
E.g. salivating when students hear the recess bell ring

name: Acquisition
q: What is acquisition in classical conditioning?
ans:
Repeated pairing of the NS and the UCS
The process of acquiring the learning

name: Principles of classical conditioning
q: What are the principles that make classical conditioning work?
ans:
CS must come before the UCS
CS and UCS close together in time (ideally only several seconds apart)
NS paired with the UCS several, often many, times
CS needs to be distinctive

name: Stimulus generalisation
q: What is stimulus generalisation, and what did Hovland's study show?
ans:
Tendency to respond to a stimulus that is only similar to the original CS
Hovland (1937): electric shock (UCS) → galvanic skin response (UCR), conditioned to tone 0
The closer a test tone's frequency to tone 0, the bigger the skin response

name: Stimulus discrimination
q: What is stimulus discrimination and why does it happen?
ans:
Tendency to stop making a generalised response to a similar stimulus
Because the similar stimulus is never paired with the UCS

name: Extinction (classical)
q: What is extinction in classical conditioning and why does it happen?
ans:
Disappearance or weakening of a learned response
Happens when the UCS no longer follows the CS
Removing the UCS stops reinforcing the CS–CR association

name: Spontaneous recovery
q: What is spontaneous recovery and what does it show about learning?
ans:
Reappearance of a learned response after extinction has occurred
Shows learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour
Also happens in operant conditioning

name: Higher-order conditioning
q: How does higher-order conditioning work?
ans:
A strong conditioned stimulus is paired with a neutral stimulus
The neutral stimulus becomes a second conditioned stimulus

name: Cognitive perspective on conditioning
q: What is the cognitive perspective on conditioning, and what did Rescorla's study show?
ans:
Conditioning works because the CS gives information / an expectancy that the UCS is coming
Rescorla (1988): two groups of rats, sustained tone + electric shock
Shock after the tone's onset: fear of the tone starting
Shock after the tone stops: fear of the tone stopping

name: Conditioned emotional response (CER)
q: What is a conditioned emotional response (CER)? Give an example.
ans:
Emotional response classically conditioned to occur to learned stimuli
E.g. fear of dogs; the reaction when seeing an attractive person
Can lead to phobias (irrational fear responses)

name: Vicarious conditioning
q: What is vicarious conditioning?
ans:
Classical conditioning of a reflex response or emotion
By watching the reaction of another person

name: Little Albert
q: What did Watson's Little Albert study do and demonstrate?
ans:
Watson conditioned a child to fear a white rat
Paired the white rat with a loud noise (naturally scary for him)
Also showed fear of a rabbit, a dog and a sealskin coat

name: Conditioned taste aversion
q: What is conditioned taste aversion and how is it formed?
ans:
Nausea or aversive response to a particular taste
Because the taste was followed by a nausea reaction
Occurs after only one association

name: Biological preparedness
q: What is biological preparedness and why does it occur?
ans:
Tendency of animals to learn certain associations (e.g. taste + nausea)
With only one or a few pairings
Because of the survival value of the learning

name: Operant conditioning
q: What is operant conditioning?
ans:
Learning of voluntary behaviour
Through the effects of pleasant and unpleasant consequences to responses
Depends on what happens after a response

name: Thorndike's law of effect
q: What is Thorndike's law of effect, and how did his puzzle box show it?
ans:
Response followed by a pleasurable consequence tends to be repeated
Response followed by an unpleasant consequence tends not to be repeated
Puzzle box: cat steps on a lever to unlock the door

name: B.F. Skinner
q: What were B.F. Skinner's main ideas and contributions to operant conditioning?
ans:
Behaviourist: studied only observable, measurable behaviour
Gave operant conditioning its name
Learning depends on the consequence: "If I do this, what's in it for me?"
Skinner box: rat presses a bar to get food

name: Reinforcement
q: What is reinforcement in operant conditioning?
ans:
Any event or stimulus that follows a response
And increases the probability that the response will occur again

name: Primary vs secondary reinforcer
q: How do primary and secondary reinforcers differ? Give examples of each.
ans:
Primary: naturally reinforcing, meets a basic biological need (hunger, thirst, touch)
Secondary: becomes reinforcing after being paired with a primary reinforcer (praise, tokens, gold stars)

name: Positive reinforcement
q: What is positive reinforcement? Give an example.
ans:
Reinforcing a response by adding a pleasurable stimulus
E.g. getting money for working; praise or merit points for wearing a seat belt
Increases the behaviour

name: Negative reinforcement
q: What is negative reinforcement? Give an example.
ans:
Reinforcing a response by removing, escaping or avoiding an unpleasant stimulus
E.g. turning in a tax return on time to avoid a penalty; seat belt stops the alarm
Also increases the behaviour

name: Continuous vs partial reinforcement
q: How does continuous reinforcement differ from partial reinforcement, and what is the partial reinforcement effect?
ans:
Continuous: reinforcement for every correct response
Partial reinforcement effect: a response reinforced after some (not all) correct responses is very resistant to extinction

name: Fixed interval schedule
q: How does a fixed interval schedule work and what pattern does it produce?
ans:
Time that must pass before reinforcement is possible is always the same
E.g. pay day
Pause after each reinforcement (scalloped graph)

name: Variable interval schedule
q: How does a variable interval schedule work and what pattern does it produce?
ans:
Time that must pass before reinforcement is possible is different each trial
Reinforcement is unpredictable, so there's no pause after it

name: Fixed ratio schedule
q: How does a fixed ratio schedule work and what pattern does it produce?
ans:
Number of responses needed for reinforcement is always the same
E.g. coffee loyalty card: buy 9, get 1 free
Pause after each reinforcement (stair-step graph)

name: Variable ratio schedule
q: How does a variable ratio schedule work and what pattern does it produce?
ans:
Number of responses needed for reinforcement is different each time
E.g. slot machines
Unpredictable, so no pause; fast response rate

name: Effectiveness of reinforcement
q: What factors make reinforcement effective?
ans:
Timing: give the reinforcer as soon as possible after the behaviour (especially animals and small children)
Delayed reinforcement can work for older children and adults
Specificity: reinforce only the desired behaviour

name: Punishment
q: What is punishment in operant conditioning?
ans:
Any event or object that follows a response
And makes that response less likely to happen again

name: Positive punishment
q: What is positive punishment? Give an example.
ans:
Punishment by application
Adding an unpleasant stimulus after a response
E.g. getting a saman (ticket) for not wearing a seat belt

name: Negative punishment
q: What is negative punishment? Give an example.
ans:
Punishment by removal
Removing a pleasurable stimulus after a response
E.g. paying a fine, losing your driving licence, being grounded

name: Problems with severe punishment
q: What are the problems with using severe punishment?
ans:
May cause avoidance of the punisher instead of the behaviour
May encourage lying to avoid punishment
Creates fear and anxiety
Models aggression

name: Making punishment effective
q: How can punishment be made more effective?
ans:
Punishment should immediately follow the behaviour
Punishment should be consistent
Pair punishing the wrong behaviour with reinforcing the right behaviour

name: Discriminative stimulus
q: What is a discriminative stimulus in operant conditioning?
ans:
Any stimulus that gives the organism a cue for making a certain response
In order to obtain reinforcement
Specific cues lead to specific responses

name: Extinction, generalisation & recovery in operant conditioning
q: How do extinction, generalisation and spontaneous recovery work in operant conditioning?
ans:
Extinction: behaviour stops if it is not reinforced (e.g. ignoring a child's tantrum)
Generalisation: responses spread to similar, not identical, stimuli
Spontaneous recovery of an extinguished response also happens

name: Shaping
q: What is shaping, and what is successive approximation?
ans:
Reinforcement of simple steps leading to a desired complex behaviour
Successive approximation: small steps, one after another, towards the goal behaviour

name: Instinctive drift
q: What is instinctive drift? Give an example.
ans:
Tendency for an animal's behaviour to revert to genetically controlled patterns
Instincts differ from species to species
Some responses can't be trained regardless of conditioning
E.g. raccoons dunking food in water

name: Behaviour modification
q: What is behaviour modification?
ans:
Using operant (sometimes classical) conditioning techniques
To bring about desired changes in behaviour

name: Token economy
q: What is a token economy? Give an example.
ans:
Type of behaviour modification
Desired behaviour is rewarded with tokens
E.g. token board, reward chart

name: Time-out
q: What is time-out and why does it work as punishment?
ans:
Mild punishment by removal
Misbehaving animal, child or adult is placed in a special area away from others' attention
Removes the chance of positive reinforcement through attention

name: Applied behaviour analysis (ABA)
q: What is applied behaviour analysis (ABA)?
ans:
Modern term for a form of behaviour modification
Uses shaping techniques to mould a desired behaviour or response

name: Biofeedback
q: What is biofeedback and what does it allow people to do?
ans:
Feedback about biological conditions
Brings involuntary responses (e.g. blood pressure, relaxation) under voluntary control

name: Neurofeedback
q: What is neurofeedback and how does it work?
ans:
Form of biofeedback using devices (EEG, fMRI)
Gives feedback about brain activity to modify behaviour

name: Operant vs classical conditioning
q: How does operant conditioning differ from classical conditioning?
ans:
Operant: increases the rate of an existing response; classical: creates a new response to a stimulus
Operant responses are voluntary (emitted); classical are involuntary, reflexive (elicited)
Operant: consequences matter; classical: antecedent stimuli matter
Operant: reinforcement immediate; classical: CS just before UCS
Operant: expect reinforcement after a correct response; classical: expect UCS after CS

name: Cognitive learning theory
q: What is cognitive learning theory, why did it emerge, and what does it cover?
ans:
Early behaviourism focused only on observable, measurable behaviour
In the 1950s and 1960s, many psychologists became aware that cognition could no longer be ignored
Cognitive learning theories study the mental events behind learning
Covers latent learning, insight learning and learned helplessness

name: Cognition
q: What is cognition?
ans: Mental events that take place inside a person's mind while behaving

name: Edward Tolman
q: Who was Edward Tolman and what is his best-known learning experiment?
ans:
Early cognitive scientist
Best-known learning experiment: taught three groups of rats the same maze, one at a time (Tolman & Honzik, 1930)
Showed latent learning

name: Latent learning
q: What is latent learning, and how did Tolman demonstrate it?
ans:
Learning that remains hidden until its application becomes useful
Shown by Tolman's maze experiment: rats learned the maze without a reward, but only showed it once a reward was given

name: Tolman & Honzik's maze experiment (1930)
q: What was the procedure and results of Tolman and Honzik's maze experiment?
ans:
A rat is placed in the start box; the trial ends when it reaches the end box
Group 1: rewarded each time at the end of the maze → learned the maze quickly
Group 2: rewarded for the first time on Day 11 → showed learning almost immediately after the reward
Group 3: never rewarded → did not show learning of the maze
Outcome measured as mean number of errors per day

name: Why Group 2 matters in Tolman's maze
q: In Tolman's maze experiment, why are Group 2's results important?
ans:
Group 2 got food for the first time on Day 11
Their errors dropped immediately on Day 12, to the level of (and then below) Group 1
They must have already learned the maze on Days 1–10 without a reward
The learning was hidden (latent) until the reward made it useful

name: Wolfgang Köhler
q: Who was Wolfgang Köhler and what did he study?
ans:
Studied ape intelligence (e.g. chimpanzees using sticks and stacking boxes to reach food)
Described insight learning

name: Insight
q: What is insight learning, and how does it differ from trial and error?
clues: relationships among parts of a problem
ans:
The sudden perception of relationships among various parts of a problem
Allows the solution to the problem to come quickly
Cannot be gained through trial-and-error learning alone
The "aha" moment

name: Martin Seligman
q: Who is Martin Seligman and what is he known for?
ans:
Played a significant role in developing the field of positive psychology
First observed learned helplessness, with Steven Maier
Known for his dog experiment

name: Learned helplessness
q: What is learned helplessness and who first observed it?
ans:
Tendency to fail to act to escape from a situation
Because of a history of repeated failures in the past
First observed by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier

name: Seligman's experiment: the two groups
q: What were the two groups in Seligman's learned helplessness experiment?
ans:
Group A: dogs heard a tone followed by a harmless but painful electric shock
Group A dogs were held in a harness so they could not escape
The assumption was that the dogs would learn to fear the tone and escape from it
Group B: control group, no conditioning to fear the tone

name: Seligman's apparatus: the two-sided box
q: What happened when Seligman's dogs were placed in the two-sided box?
ans:
Dogs from both groups were placed in a two-sided box with a hurdle in the middle
Dogs with no prior experience of inescapable shock quickly jumped the hurdle to the "safe side"
Dogs that had learned escape was impossible stayed on the side where the shock occurred
They did not even try to go over the hurdle → learned helplessness

name: Albert Bandura
q: Who was Albert Bandura and what is he known for?
ans:
Studied observational learning
Known for the Bobo doll experiment
Proposed the learning/performance distinction

name: Observational learning
q: What is observational learning?
ans:
Learning new behaviour by watching a model perform that behaviour
Albert Bandura

name: Learning/performance distinction
q: What is the learning/performance distinction?
ans:
Learning can take place without actual performance of the learned behaviour
The behaviour may only be shown later, e.g. when there is a reason (reward) to perform it

name: Bobo doll experiment
q: What were the conditions and findings of Bandura's Bobo doll experiment?
ans:
Condition 1: model plays with the toys in a nonaggressive way and ignores the Bobo doll
Condition 2: model is aggressive with the doll: kicking, yelling, throwing and hitting it with a hammer
Children who watched the aggressive model tended to imitate the aggression
Raises questions about aggression, prosocial behaviour and the media

name: Bobo doll: model rewarded vs punished
q: In later Bobo doll studies, how did rewarding or punishing the model affect children?
ans:
Later studies: the model was either rewarded or punished for the aggressive behaviour
Children who saw the model rewarded imitated without prompting
Children who saw the model punished did not imitate unless the experimenter rewarded them
Consequences matter for motivation (and those children had still learned the behaviour)

name: Four elements of observational learning
q: What are the four elements of observational learning?
ans:
Attention
Memory / retention
Imitation / motoric reproduction processes
Desire / motivation

name: Attention (observational learning)
q: What role does attention play in observational learning?
ans:
To learn anything through observation, the learner must first pay attention to the model
Distinctive features of the model help capture attention

name: Memory / retention (observational learning)
q: What role does memory or retention play in observational learning? Give an example.
ans:
The learner must be able to retain the memory of what was done
E.g. remembering the steps for a dish first seen on a cooking show

name: Imitation / motoric reproduction (observational learning)
q: What role does imitation or motoric reproduction play in observational learning?
ans: The learner must be capable of reproducing, or imitating, the actions of the model

name: Desire / motivation (observational learning)
q: What role does desire or motivation play in observational learning?
ans:
The learner must have the motivation to perform the action
Motivation is low to imitate models who fail or are punished
Motivation is high if rewards are expected

name: Santiago Ramón y Cajal
q: Who was Santiago Ramón y Cajal and what did he theorise about nerve cells?
ans:
Spaniard (1852–1934)
First to theorise that the individual cells of the nervous system remain separate

name: CNS vs PNS
q: How does the central nervous system (CNS) differ from the peripheral nervous system (PNS)?
ans:
Central nervous system (CNS): brain + spinal cord
Peripheral nervous system (PNS): nerves that run through the body itself

name: Neuron vs glial cells
q: How do neurons differ from glial cells?
ans:
Neuron: receives and sends messages within the nervous system
Glial cells: major support structures of the nervous system

name: Soma & nucleus
q: What do the soma and the nucleus of a neuron do?
ans:
Soma (cell body): responsible for maintaining the life of the cell
Nucleus: contains the chromosomes

name: Dendrites
q: What is the function of dendrites?
ans: Receive messages from other neurons

name: Axon & axon terminals
q: What do the axon and the axon terminals do?
ans:
Axon: carries messages from the soma to the axon terminals
Axon terminals: communicate with other cells

name: Myelin sheath
q: What is the myelin sheath and what does it do?
ans:
Fatty substance coating the axon
Insulates, protects and speeds up neural impulses

name: Cell membrane
q: What is the function of the neuron's cell membrane?
ans: Separates the inside of the cell from the outside environment

name: Sensory neuron
q: What does a sensory neuron do, and what is its other name?
ans:
Carries information from the senses to the CNS
Activated by sensory input, e.g. touching a hot surface
Also called an afferent neuron (receiving information)

name: Motor neuron
q: What does a motor neuron do, and what is its other name?
ans:
Carries messages from the CNS to the muscles of the body
Transmits impulses from the spinal cord to skeletal and smooth muscles; controls all muscle movement
Also called an efferent neuron (sending out information)

name: Interneuron
q: Where are interneurons found and what do they do?
ans:
Found in the centre of the spinal cord
Receives information from sensory neurons and sends commands to muscles through motor neurons
Makes up the bulk of neurons in the brain

name: Astrocytes
q: What are the functions of astrocytes?
ans:
Help synchronise the activity of axons
Remove waste when neurons die
Control blood flow to each brain area; dilate blood vessels for more nutrients during heightened activity

name: Microglia
q: What do microglia do?
ans:
Remove waste, viruses, fungi and other harmful microorganisms
Work like an immune system

name: Oligodendrocytes vs Schwann cells
q: How do oligodendrocytes differ from Schwann cells, and what do they share?
ans:
Both build the myelin sheath around some axons
Oligodendrocytes: in the CNS; more likely to be permanently damaged
Schwann cells: in the PNS; can reconnect and repair themselves if damaged

name: Radial glia
q: What do radial glia do during brain development, and what do they become?
ans:
Guide the migration of neurons and the growth of axons and dendrites during early brain development
Most later turn into neurons, some into other glial cells

name: Ion channels & sodium-potassium pump
q: How do ion channels and the sodium-potassium pump work?
ans:
Many channels are gated: open or close depending on conditions (e.g. electrical potential)
Sodium and potassium channels
Sodium-potassium pump: pushes 3 sodium ions out, draws 2 potassium ions in
The pump needs energy (ATP)

name: Semipermeable membrane
q: What does it mean that the neuron's membrane is semipermeable?
ans:
Some molecules pass freely through the membrane
Others need channels or pumps to enter or exit

name: Resting potential
q: What is the resting potential, and how are ions distributed during it?
ans:
State of a neuron not firing
Negatively charged inside: −70 mV
Inside: more negative anions and potassium ions; outside: more sodium and chloride ions
Sodium and potassium channels are closed
The electrical gradient sets the stage for a rapid action potential

name: Action potential
q: What is an action potential?
ans:
The release of a neural impulse
A reversal of the electrical charge inside the axon (negative → positive)
A rapid series, each lasting about a millisecond

name: Steps of an action potential
q: What happens at each step of an action potential?
ans:
Strong enough stimulus: sodium and potassium channels open
Sodium rushes in, neuron becomes positive (depolarisation)
Sodium channels close at the peak; potassium channels stay open
Potassium rushes out, then its channels close: hyperpolarisation (below resting)
Sodium-potassium pump restores the resting potential

name: Depolarisation vs hyperpolarisation
q: How does depolarisation differ from hyperpolarisation?
ans:
Depolarisation: sodium rushes in, the neuron becomes positively charged
Hyperpolarisation: potassium rushes out, the charge goes beyond the original resting potential

name: Threshold of excitement
q: What is the threshold of excitement and why does it matter?
ans:
Level above which any stimulation produces a massive depolarisation
No action potential if the threshold isn't reached

name: All-or-none law
q: What does the all-or-none law state?
ans: An action potential fires at full strength or not at all

name: Coding stimulus strength
q: How does a neuron signal the strength of a stimulus?
ans:
Action potentials are equal in intensity and speed within a neuron
A stronger stimulus can't make bigger or faster action potentials
Strength is signalled by the frequency of firing and the number of neurons firing

name: Absolute vs relative refractory period
q: What is the refractory period, and how do its absolute and relative phases differ?
ans:
Refractory period: neuron resists producing more action potentials
Absolute: impossible to fire again, regardless of stimulation
Relative: needs a stronger-than-usual stimulus to fire

name: Axon hillock
q: What is the axon hillock and what role does it play?
clues: swelling where the axon leaves the soma
ans:
Where the action potential begins
A swelling where the axon exits the soma

name: Propagation of the action potential
q: How does an action potential propagate along the axon?
ans:
Sodium ions enter one point on the axon
Positive ions flow to neighbouring regions and slightly depolarise the next part of the membrane
That area reaches threshold and opens its voltage-gated sodium channels

name: Nodes of Ranvier & saltatory conduction
q: What are nodes of Ranvier and what is saltatory conduction?
ans:
Nodes of Ranvier: short unmyelinated gaps in the myelin sheath
The action potential is regenerated at each node
Saltatory conduction: the action potential jumps from node to node, increasing speed

name: Synapse
q: What is a synapse?
ans:
Site where nerve impulses pass between two nerve cells
Neurons communicate by transmitting chemicals at synapses

name: Presynaptic vs postsynaptic neuron
q: How does the presynaptic neuron differ from the postsynaptic neuron?
ans:
Presynaptic neuron: delivers the synaptic transmission
Postsynaptic neuron: receives the message

name: Charles Sherrington
q: Who was Charles Sherrington and what did he contribute to understanding synapses?
ans:
Coined the term synapse in 1906 for the gap between neurons
Studied how neurons communicate using reflexes in dogs

name: Sherrington's 3 findings about reflexes
q: What were Sherrington's three findings about reflexes, and what did they suggest?
ans:
Reflexes are slower than conduction along an axon (≈40 m/s vs ≈15 m/s or less)
Several weak stimuli at slightly different times or places give a stronger reflex than one
As one set of muscles relaxes, another set becomes excited
All suggested special processes at the synapse

name: Temporal summation
q: What is temporal summation?
ans:
Repeated stimuli over a short time have a cumulative effect
Can trigger a nerve impulse when a single stimulus is too weak

name: Spatial summation
q: What is spatial summation?
ans:
Synaptic input from several locations has a cumulative effect
Can trigger a nerve impulse when a single stimulus would not

name: EPSP
q: What is an EPSP and how does it affect firing?
ans:
Excitatory postsynaptic potential
Positive ions flow into the postsynaptic cell, making an action potential more likely
A graded depolarisation that decays quickly if threshold isn't reached
Adding up EPSPs is the basis of temporal and spatial summation

name: IPSP
q: What is an IPSP and how does it affect the neuron?
ans:
Inhibitory postsynaptic potential: temporary hyperpolarisation of the membrane
Potassium ions leave or chloride ions enter the cell
Acts as an active brake that suppresses excitation

name: EPSP vs IPSP ratio
q: What determines whether a neuron fires when it receives both EPSPs and IPSPs?
ans:
Neurons can have thousands of synapses
Temporal and spatial summation can happen within one neuron
Whether an action potential fires depends on the ratio of IPSPs to EPSPs at that moment

name: Otto Loewi's experiment
q: What did Otto Loewi's experiment involve and what did it show?
ans:
Stimulated the vagus nerve, and the frog's heart rate decreased
Collected the fluid and transferred it to another frog's heart
That heart rate also decreased
Showed communication across the synapse is chemical

name: Neurotransmitter
q: What are neurotransmitters, and when was chemical transmission established as the main type?
ans:
Chemicals that travel across the synapse and allow neurons to communicate
Chemical transmission was established as the main type only around 1950

name: Synthesis & storage
q: How are neurotransmitters synthesised and where are they stored?
ans:
Neurons synthesise neurotransmitters (smaller in axon terminals, larger in the cell body)
Stored in axon terminals in synaptic vesicles (saclike structures in the presynaptic terminal)

name: Release & exocytosis
q: How are neurotransmitters released, and what is exocytosis?
ans:
An action potential causes calcium to enter the terminal
This releases neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft
Exocytosis: excretion of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic terminal into the cleft

name: Receptor sites
q: What happens at receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron?
ans:
Neurotransmitters cross the cleft and attach to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron
Receptor sites: proteins on dendrites (or muscle/gland cells) shaped to fit only certain neurotransmitters

name: Reuptake vs enzymatic degradation
q: How does reuptake differ from enzymatic degradation of neurotransmitters?
ans:
Neurotransmitters separate from receptors so the next stimulation can occur
Reuptake: taken back into the presynaptic neuron's vesicles
Enzymatic degradation: structure altered so it can't act on a receptor
E.g. monoamine oxidase (MAO) breaks down serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine

name: Acetylcholine (ACh)
q: What are the effects and functions of acetylcholine (ACh)?
ans:
Excitatory or inhibitory
Arousal, attention, memory; controls muscle contractions
Stimulates skeletal muscles to contract but slows heart muscle
In the hippocampus, plays a role in memory

name: Dopamine & norepinephrine
q: What are the functions of dopamine and norepinephrine, and what disorders involve dopamine?
ans:
Dopamine: excitatory or inhibitory; control of movement and pleasure
Too little in certain areas: Parkinson's disease; too much in others: schizophrenia
Norepinephrine: mainly excitatory; arousal and mood

name: Serotonin, GABA, glutamate & endorphins
q: What are the main functions of serotonin, GABA, glutamate and endorphins?
ans:
Serotonin (5-HT): sleep, mood, anxiety, appetite
GABA: major inhibitory; sleep, inhibits movement
Glutamate: major excitatory; learning, memory, development, plasticity
Endorphins: inhibitory regulators; pain relief

name: Agonist vs antagonist
q: How does an agonist differ from an antagonist, with examples of each?
ans:
Agonist: mimics or enhances a neurotransmitter's effect at the receptor
E.g. benzodiazepines (antianxiety) are GABA agonists
Antagonist: blocks or reduces the cell's response
E.g. antipsychotic drugs are dopamine antagonists

name: SSRIs & MAOIs
q: How do SSRIs and MAOIs change neurotransmitter levels in the synapse?
ans:
Some drugs change the amount of neurotransmitter in the synapse
SSRIs: block the reuptake of serotonin
MAOIs: block monoamine oxidase, so less neurotransmitter is broken down

name: Postsynaptic receptors
q: What happens when a neurotransmitter binds to postsynaptic receptors?
ans:
Neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
Activation opens ion channels; ions flow in or out
The result (EPSP or IPSP) depends on which channel opens
Effect also depends on ionotropic vs metabotropic receptors

name: Ionotropic effect
q: What is an ionotropic effect, and what are its speed, uses and neurotransmitters?
ans:
Neurotransmitter attaches and immediately opens ion channels (ligand-gated)
Very fast (< 1 ms), very short (half-life ≈ 5 ms)
Suits information that must update quickly, e.g. vision
Mostly glutamate, ACh (excitatory) or GABA, glycine (inhibitory)

name: Metabotropic effect
q: What is a metabotropic effect, and how does it work?
ans:
Starts a slower, longer-lasting chain of metabolic reactions (~30 ms; lasts seconds to minutes)
Uses many neurotransmitters, e.g. serotonin, dopamine
Suits enduring effects: taste, smell, attention
Receptor bends, releasing a G-protein that raises a second messenger (e.g. cyclic AMP)
The second messenger can open/close channels, alter proteins or activate chromosomes

name: Hormone
q: What is a hormone and how does it act on the body?
ans:
A chemical secreted by a gland or other cells
Carried by the blood to other organs, where it alters activity
Made by endocrine glands; triggers long-lasting changes across the body

name: Key hormones by gland
q: What are the key hormones released by each major gland, and what do they do?
ans:
Posterior pituitary: oxytocin (contractions, milk release), vasopressin (raises blood pressure)
Pineal: melatonin (sleepiness)
Adrenal cortex: cortisol (raises blood sugar and metabolism)
Adrenal medulla: epinephrine, norepinephrine (like the sympathetic NS)
Pancreas: insulin, glucagon; fat cells: leptin (decreases appetite)

name: Negative feedback
q: What is negative feedback in the endocrine system, with an example?
ans:
A product feeds back to decrease its own production
Brings things back to normal when they become too extreme
Example: the thyroid (hypothalamus → pituitary → thyroid loop)

name: Superior/inferior & anterior/posterior
q: What do the terms superior/inferior and anterior/posterior mean?
ans:
Superior: towards the top; inferior: towards the bottom
Anterior: towards the front; posterior: towards the back

name: Dorsal/ventral & rostral/caudal
q: What do the terms dorsal/ventral and rostral/caudal mean?
ans:
Dorsal: towards the back or top of the head; ventral: towards the stomach
Rostral: towards the nose; caudal: towards the tail

name: Medial/lateral & ipsilateral/contralateral
q: What do medial/lateral and ipsilateral/contralateral mean?
ans:
Medial: towards the middle; lateral: towards the side
Ipsilateral: same side of the body; contralateral: opposite side

name: Planes of the brain
q: What are the three planes of the brain and how is each sliced?
ans:
Coronal plane: front-to-back slices
Horizontal plane: top-to-bottom slices
Sagittal plane: side-to-side slices

name: Peripheral nervous system (PNS)
q: What is the peripheral nervous system (PNS) and what are its two parts?
ans:
All nerves and neurons not in the brain and spinal cord, running through the body
Two parts: somatic and autonomic nervous systems

name: Somatic nervous system
q: What does the somatic nervous system control, and what are its two pathways?
ans:
Controls the voluntary muscles of the body
Sensory pathway: messages from the senses to the CNS (afferent)
Motor pathway: from the CNS to voluntary muscles (efferent)

name: Autonomic nervous system
q: What does the autonomic nervous system control, and what are its divisions?
ans:
Controls involuntary muscles, organs and glands
E.g. heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, digestion
Two divisions: sympathetic and parasympathetic

name: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic
q: How does the sympathetic nervous system differ from the parasympathetic?
ans:
Sympathetic: reacts to stress and arousal; prepares organs for rigorous activity (fight-or-flight)
Parasympathetic: restores the body after arousal; day-to-day functioning
Parasympathetic lowers heart rate, increases digestion, conserves energy (eat-drink-and-rest)

name: Spinal cord
q: What is the spinal cord's role, and how do its grey and white matter differ?
ans:
Inside the spinal column; communicates with sense organs and muscles below the head
Grey matter: centre, packed with cell bodies and dendrites; responsible for reflexes
White matter: mostly myelinated axons carrying information to the brain or along the cord

name: Medulla
q: Where is the medulla and what does it do?
ans:
First large swelling at the top of the spinal cord; lowest part of the brain
Life-sustaining functions: breathing, swallowing, heart rate

name: Pons
q: Where is the pons and what does it do?
ans:
Larger swelling just above the medulla
Connects the cerebellum with the top of the brain
Part in sleep, dreaming and arousal

name: Reticular formation
q: Where is the reticular formation and what is it responsible for?
ans:
Area of neurons running through the middle of the medulla and pons
Responsible for attention, alertness and arousal

name: Cerebellum
q: Where is the cerebellum, what does it do, and what happens when it's damaged?
ans:
Behind the pons, with many deep folds
Regulates rapid movement, balance and coordination; stores learned reflexes, skills and habits
Also attention shifting and sensory timing
Damage: clumsiness, poor balance, slurred speech, timing difficulty

name: Brain stem
q: What makes up the brain stem and the hindbrain?
ans:
Hindbrain structures, the midbrain and other structures together make up the brain stem
Hindbrain = medulla, pons, cerebellum (posterior part of the brain)

name: Tectum & colliculi
q: What are the tectum and the superior and inferior colliculi responsible for?
ans:
Tectum: roof of the midbrain
Superior colliculus: vision
Inferior colliculus: hearing

name: Tegmentum & substantia nigra
q: What are the tegmentum and substantia nigra, and what do they do?
ans:
Tegmentum: intermediate level; part of the reticular formation and pathways between forebrain and spinal cord
Substantia nigra: gives rise to the dopamine pathway for readiness to move

name: Forebrain
q: What is the forebrain and how is it organised?
ans:
Most anterior and prominent part of the mammalian brain
Two cerebral hemispheres: outer cerebral cortex plus subcortical regions
Each side controls the opposite (contralateral) side of the body

name: Limbic system
q: What is the limbic system, which structures does it include, and what does it do?
ans:
Interlinked structures forming a border around the brainstem
Thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate cortex
Involved in emotion, motivation, memory and learning

name: Thalamus
q: Where is the thalamus, what does it do, and what does damage cause?
ans:
Pair of structures in the centre of the forebrain
Relay station: most sensory information goes through it to the cortex (except smell)
Damage: loss or partial loss of sensations

name: Hypothalamus
q: Where is the hypothalamus and what does it regulate?
ans:
Very small, below and in front of the thalamus, above the pituitary gland
Signals the pituitary to change hormone release
Regulates temperature, eating, drinking, sleep-wake, sexual behaviour, emotion

name: Hippocampus, amygdala & cingulate cortex
q: What do the hippocampus, amygdala and cingulate cortex each do?
ans:
Hippocampus (seahorse-shaped, medial temporal lobe): forms long-term declarative memories
Amygdala (almond-shaped, near the hippocampus): fear responses and fear memory
Cingulate cortex (above the corpus callosum): emotional and cognitive processing

name: Basal ganglia
q: What structures make up the basal ganglia and what are their functions?
ans:
Caudate nucleus, putamen and globus pallidus
Mainly motor control; also motor learning and executive functions

name: Ventricles & cerebrospinal fluid
q: What are the central canal, ventricles and cerebrospinal fluid?
ans:
Central canal: fluid-filled channel in the centre of the spinal cord
Ventricles: four fluid-filled cavities in the brain
Cerebrospinal fluid: clear fluid that cushions the brain and stores hormones and nutrients

name: Hemispheres & corpus callosum
q: How are the cerebral hemispheres connected, and how is information sent to each side?
ans:
Cerebrum: two hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum
Contralateral: each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body
Bilateral: information to both sides (hearing, vision)
Ipsilateral: same side (taste, smell)

name: Occipital lobe
q: Where is the occipital lobe and what do its cortical areas do?
ans:
At the rear and bottom of each hemisphere; visual centres of the brain
Primary visual cortex: processes visual information
Visual association cortex: makes sense of visual information

name: Parietal lobe
q: Where is the parietal lobe and what does it process?
ans:
At the top and back of each hemisphere; touch, taste and temperature
Somatosensory cortex: processes skin and body-position information

name: Temporal lobe
q: Where is the temporal lobe and what are its functions?
ans:
Along the sides of the brain, just behind the temples
Hearing and meaningful speech
Primary auditory cortex and auditory association cortex
Also language, learning, memory and some visual processing

name: Frontal lobe & motor cortex
q: Where is the frontal lobe, what does it do, and what is the motor cortex's role?
ans:
In the front and top of the brain
Higher mental processes: planning, personality, decision-making; fluent speech production
Motor cortex: sends motor commands to the muscles of the somatic NS

name: Prefrontal cortex & Phineas Gage
q: What does the prefrontal cortex do, and what does Phineas Gage's case show?
ans:
Executive functions for goal-directed problem solving: working memory, inhibition, flexibility, self-control
Regulates impulsive behaviour and controls complex behaviour
Phineas Gage: injury to the left PFC led to personality change, impulsivity, lack of inhibition

name: Broca's vs Wernicke's area
q: How do Broca's and Wernicke's areas and their aphasias differ?
ans:
Broca's area (left frontal lobe): fluent speech
Broca's aphasia: understands others but can't pronounce words accurately
Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe): understanding word meaning
Wernicke's aphasia: speaks smoothly but without coherent meaning

name: Lesioning & brain stimulation (ESB)
q: What are lesioning and electrical stimulation of the brain (ESB)?
clues: destroy cells at a wire tip
ans:
Lesioning: an electric current through a thin wire destroys brain cells at its tip
Deliberate damage in animals, or case studies of humans with brain damage
Electrical stimulation of the brain (ESB): milder current makes neurons act as if they got a message

name: DBS vs TMS vs tDCS
q: How do DBS, TMS and tDCS differ?
ans:
Deep brain stimulation (invasive): implanted generator sends impulses to implanted electrodes
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (noninvasive): magnetic pulses via coils over the head
Transcranial direct current stimulation (noninvasive): very low current through scalp electrodes

name: Mapping structure: CT vs MRI
q: How do CT and MRI differ for mapping brain structure?
ans:
CT: computer-controlled X-rays; detects tumours, injuries, abnormal structure; suitable with metal in the body
MRI: radio waves and magnetic fields give detailed images; good spatial resolution

name: Mapping function: EEG vs PET vs fMRI
q: How do EEG, PET and fMRI differ for mapping brain function?
ans:
EEG: electrical activity via scalp electrodes; good temporal, poor spatial resolution
PET: injected radioactive glucose shows which cells are active
fMRI: magnetic field tracks brain oxygenation; more oxygen = more activity; clearer detail

name: Thinking (cognition)
q: What is thinking (cognition), and what does it involve?
ans:
Mental activity in the brain when a person is processing information
Includes organising, understanding and communicating information
More than a stream of consciousness; words and images are often involved

name: Mental images
q: What are mental images and how do they help us?
ans:
Mental representations of objects or events with a picture-like quality
Help identify properties of imagined objects (which is darker green?)
Help us navigate, track and reach

name: Kosslyn et al. (1978)
q: What did Kosslyn et al.'s (1978) mental map study show?
ans:
Participants mentally 'travelled' between places on a memorised map
The greater the physical distance, the longer it took to reach the place
Mental images keep spatial properties like real pictures

name: Mental rotation & imagery vs perception
q: What is mental rotation, and how does imagery differ from perception in the brain?
ans:
Mental rotation: turning an imagined object to compare it
Perception and imagery activate the same lobes (frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital)
Perception: faster, bottom-up, stronger visual cortex activity
Imagery: slower, top-down, weaker visual cortex activity

name: Concept
q: What is a concept? Give an example.
ans:
An idea representing a class or category of objects, events or activities
E.g. thinking 'fruit' without thinking of every fruit
Contains key features, so new examples can be identified

name: Formal vs natural concepts
q: How do formal concepts differ from natural concepts? Give examples.
ans:
Formal: defined by specific rules or features (e.g. a square)
Natural: formed from real-world experience, not strict rules; tend to be fuzzy
Natural concept examples: platypus as a mammal, raft as a vehicle

name: Prototype
q: What is a prototype and how does it develop? Give an example.
ans:
An example that closely matches a concept's defining characteristics
Develops from exposure to objects in that category
E.g. Northern Hemisphere 'fruit': apple, pear, orange rather than durian or guava

name: Schemas & scripts
q: What are schemas and scripts?
ans:
Schemas: mental generalisations about objects, places, events and people
Scripts: a type of schema for a familiar sequence of activities

name: Problem-solving vs decision-making
q: How does problem-solving differ from decision-making?
ans:
Problem-solving: reaching a goal by thinking and behaving in certain ways
Decision-making: identifying, evaluating and choosing between alternatives
Problem-solving is part of decision-making

name: Trial and error vs algorithms
q: How does trial and error differ from using an algorithm in problem-solving?
ans:
Trial and error (mechanical solution): try one solution after another until one works
Algorithm: specific step-by-step procedure; always finds the correct solution if one exists (e.g. maths formulas)

name: Heuristic
q: What is a heuristic in problem-solving?
ans:
Educated guess from prior experience that narrows down possible solutions
A simple rule meant to apply to many situations ('rule of thumb')

name: Representativeness vs availability heuristic
q: How does the representativeness heuristic differ from the availability heuristic? Give examples.
ans:
Representativeness: assumes anything sharing a category's characteristics belongs to it
E.g. 'all Chinese people are from China'; 'you don't look like a doctor'
Availability: judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind
E.g. afraid to swim after seeing shark attacks in the news

name: Working backward & subgoals
q: How do working backward and subgoals help in problem-solving?
ans:
Working backward: start from the goal (e.g. coffee shop) and plan the route back
Subgoals: break the goal into smaller steps so each one brings the solution closer

name: Insight
q: What is insight in problem-solving and when does it often occur?
ans:
Sudden perception of a solution ('Aha!' moment)
The problem may be recognised as like one solved before
Often happens while thinking of other things (e.g. Köhler's chimpanzee)

name: Barriers to problem-solving
q: What are the three main barriers to problem-solving?
ans:
Functional fixedness: thinking of objects only in terms of their typical functions
Mental set: persisting with problem-solving patterns that worked in the past
Confirmation bias: seeking evidence that fits beliefs, ignoring evidence that doesn't

name: Convergent vs divergent thinking
q: What is creativity, and how does convergent thinking differ from divergent thinking?
ans:
Creativity: solving problems by combining ideas or behaviour in new ways
Convergent thinking: one answer, reached with previous knowledge and logic
Divergent thinking: from one point, produce many different ideas

name: Ways to think more divergently
q: What are some ways to think more divergently?
ans:
Brainstorming
Keeping a journal
Freewriting
Mind or subject mapping

name: Language
q: What is language?
ans:
A system for combining symbols (e.g. words) so that an unlimited number of meaningful statements can be made
For the purpose of communicating with others

name: Grammar, phonemes & morphemes
q: What are grammar, phonemes and morphemes? Give an example of morphemes.
ans:
Grammar: rules for language use and structure
Phonemes: basic units of sound
Morphemes: smallest units of meaning; 'playing' = play + ing

name: Syntax, semantics & pragmatics
q: What are syntax, semantics and pragmatics in language?
ans:
Syntax: rules for combining words into grammatical sentences
Semantics: rules for meaning ('Johnny hit the ball' = 'the ball was hit by Johnny')
Pragmatics: practical and social side of communication, e.g. simple language with children

name: Child-directed speech
q: What is child-directed speech and why is it useful?
ans:
How adults and older children talk to infants
Higher-pitched, repetitive, sing-song speech
Creates learning opportunities between caregiver and infant

name: Stages of language development
q: What are the stages of language development, with approximate ages?
ans:
Cooing (~2 months): vowel-like sounds
Babbling (~6 months): consonant + vowel sounds
One-word speech / holophrases (~age 1): 'Milk!'
Telegraphic speech (~age 1.5): 'Mummy go'
Whole sentences (~preschool years)

name: Piaget vs Vygotsky
q: How do Piaget and Vygotsky differ on language and thought?
ans:
Piaget: concepts come first, then language
Vygotsky: language comes first, then concepts

name: Linguistic relativity vs cognitive universalism
q: How does linguistic relativity differ from cognitive universalism, and what does the evidence show?
ans:
Linguistic relativity (Sapir-Whorf): language controls thought and concepts
Inuit 'many words for snow' turned out false; Dani (2 colour words) perceive colour like English speakers
Cognitive universalism: universal concepts shape language
Findings are mixed and inconclusive

name: Gelman & Markman (1986)
q: What did Gelman and Markman's (1986) study show about language and thought?
ans:
Children told a bird was a 'blackbird' more often said it fed its baby mashed-up food, like the other bird
The label shaped their inference more than appearance
Linguistic relativity may explain higher-level concepts rather than perception

name: Animal language & Kanzi
q: Can animals use language, and what did studies of Kanzi show?
ans:
Animals communicate by sound or behaviour; hard to judge if it's language
Communication is instinctive; human language is voluntary, deliberate and symbolic
Kanzi the chimp: recognised 150 words, followed some complex instructions
No conclusive evidence animals can master syntax

name: Bilingualism
q: What cognitive benefits are thought to come from bilingualism, and what does the evidence show?
ans:
Speaking two languages
Thought to bring less cognitive decline, better executive function, set shifting and inhibitory control
Meta-analysis (Gunnerud et al., 2020): overall advantages are negligible

name: Sensation, sensory receptors & transduction
q: What is sensation, what are sensory receptors, and what is transduction?
ans:
Sensation: special receptors in the sense organs are activated
Sensory receptors: specialised neurons stimulated by different kinds of energy, not neurotransmitters (e.g. eyes by light)
Transduction: turning outside stimuli into neural activity

name: Absolute threshold vs JND
q: How does the absolute threshold differ from the just noticeable difference (JND)?
ans:
Absolute threshold: lowest level of stimulation a person can consciously detect 50% of the time it is present
Just noticeable difference (difference threshold): smallest difference between two stimuli detectable 50% of the time

name: Absolute threshold examples
q: Give an example of the absolute threshold for each of the five senses.
ans:
Sight: a candle flame 30 miles away on a clear, dark night
Hearing: a mechanical watch ticking 20 feet away in a quiet room
Smell: one drop of perfume through a three-room apartment
Taste: 1 teaspoon of sugar in 2 gallons of water
Touch: a bee's wing falling on the cheek from 1 cm above

name: Subliminal stimuli & subliminal perception
q: What are subliminal stimuli, and what is subliminal perception?
ans:
Subliminal stimuli: below the level of conscious awareness
Strong enough to activate receptors, but not to be consciously noticed (sublimin = below the threshold)
Subliminal perception: subliminal stimuli act on the unconscious mind, possibly influencing behaviour

name: Habituation vs sensory adaptation
q: How does habituation differ from sensory adaptation? Give an example of each.
ans:
Habituation: the brain stops attending to constant, unchanging information (e.g. not hearing the classroom aircon)
Sensory adaptation: receptor cells become less responsive to an unchanging stimulus and stop sending signals (e.g. food taste fades after eating the same thing)
Microsaccades (tiny eye movements) prevent sensory adaptation in vision

name: Light: brightness, colour & saturation
q: What is light, and which wave properties give brightness, colour and saturation?
ans:
Light: a physical stimulus made of photons (wave packets) with specific wavelengths
Brightness: amplitude of the wave (higher wave = brighter)
Colour (hue): length of the wave
Saturation: perceived purity of the colour

name: Visible spectrum
q: What range of wavelengths is the visible spectrum, and which colours sit where?
ans:
Starts at about 400 nm: violet
About 500 nm: blue
Up to about 700 nm: red

name: Structure of the eye
q: What do the cornea, pupil, iris, lens, fovea and blind spot do?
ans:
Cornea: curved, transparent dome that bends incoming light so it can focus on the retina
Pupil: opening in the iris that changes size with the amount of light
Iris: coloured muscles that control the pupil
Lens: transparent disc that changes shape to bring objects into focus
Fovea: central retina, sharpest focus, most cones
Blind spot: where the optic nerve leaves the eye; no photoreceptors

name: Retina and its three layers
q: What is the retina, and what are its three layers?
ans:
Final stop for light in the eye
Ganglion cells: their axons form the optic nerve
Bipolar cells: interneurons
Photoreceptors (rods and cones): respond to light and turn it into neural activity

name: Rods vs cones
q: How do rods differ from cones in function, lighting and location?
ans:
Rods: non-colour vision in low light; work well in dim light; concentrated in the periphery
Cones: colour vision and sharpness; work best in bright light; concentrated in the fovea

name: Visual pathway
q: How does visual information travel from each visual field to the brain?
ans:
Contralateral
Left visual field → right visual cortex
Right visual field → left visual cortex

name: Trichromatic theory
q: What does the trichromatic theory say about colour vision, and who proposed it?
ans:
Proposed by Thomas Young (1802), modified by Hermann von Helmholtz (1852)
Colour vision depends on three cone types, each sensitive to a range of wavelengths
Short (≈420 nm, blue-violet), medium (≈530 nm, green), long (≈560 nm, green-yellow)
The brain works out colour from the relative activity across the three cones

name: Opponent-process theory & afterimages
q: What does the opponent-process theory say, and how does it explain afterimages?
ans:
Proposed by Ewald Hering (1874)
Visual neurons are stimulated by one colour and inhibited by another
Four primaries in opponent pairs: red–green, blue–yellow
Afterimage: stare at green → green cells fatigue; switch to white → opponent red cells are more active, so you see red

name: Colour vision deficiency
q: What causes colour vision deficiency, and how do monochromatic and dichromatic vision differ?
ans:
Caused by defective cones in the retina (genetic mutations)
Monochromatic: no colour, only shades of grey
Dichromatic: one cone type doesn't work, so colour comes from only two
Protanopia (red cones) and deuteranopia (green cones): can't tell red from green
Tritanopia (no blue cones): can't tell blue from yellow

name: Sound waves
q: Which properties of sound waves give pitch, volume and timbre, and what is the range of human hearing?
ans:
Wavelength → frequency or pitch
Amplitude → volume (soft or loud)
Purity → timbre (richness of tone)
Hertz (Hz): cycles per second
Human hearing: about 20 to 20,000 Hz

name: Inner ear: cochlea, organ of Corti & auditory nerve
q: What are the cochlea, the organ of Corti and the auditory nerve?
ans:
Cochlea: snail-shaped, fluid-filled structure of the inner ear; fluid surrounds the basilar membrane
Organ of Corti: where the hearing receptor cells (hair cells) are
Auditory nerve: bundle of axons from the hair cells; receives the message from the organ of Corti

name: Gustation and taste buds
q: How does gustation work, and where is taste processed in the brain?
ans:
Taste buds: taste receptor cells, mostly on the tongue
More taste buds = more sensitive to tastes
Each taste bud has about 20 receptors; works like neurotransmission
Taste goes to the gustatory cortex (anterior insula and frontal operculum)

name: Basic tastes
q: What are the five basic tastes, and what is the possible sixth?
ans:
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami
Umami comes from glutamate (e.g. MSG)
Possible sixth: oleogustus, the taste of fatty acids
Tastes are processed all over the tongue

name: Olfaction
q: How does olfaction work, and how is its brain pathway different from other senses?
ans:
Sense of smell; a chemical sense like taste
Olfactory receptor cells at the top of the nasal passage turn odours into neural impulses; each has cilia
Signals go straight to the olfactory bulbs, without passing through the thalamus
From the bulbs to the piriform cortex, orbitofrontal cortex and amygdala

name: Skin senses and their receptors
q: What do free nerve endings, Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Ruffini endings detect?
ans:
Skin senses (somaesthetic): touch, pressure, temperature, pain
Free nerve endings: pain, touch, temperature
Meissner's corpuscle: touch
Pacinian corpuscle: pressure
Ruffini ending: pressure and stretching

name: Gate-control theory of pain
q: What does the gate-control theory of pain say about how pain can be reduced?
ans:
Pain signals must pass through a gate in the spinal cord
Non-pain signals from the body or brain can close the gate
E.g. rubbing a sore spot inhibits pain
Endorphins inhibit pain transmission

name: Perception
q: What is perception, and how does it differ from sensation?
ans:
The way sensations at any moment are interpreted and organised in a meaningful way
E.g. two people look at the same cloud: both see it, but perceive it differently

name: Figure-ground
q: What is the figure-ground principle, and what are reversible figures?
ans:
Tendency to perceive objects (figures) as existing on a background
Reversible figures: illusions where figure and ground can switch

name: Proximity vs similarity
q: How do the Gestalt principles of proximity and similarity group objects?
ans:
Proximity: objects close to each other are seen as one group
Similarity: things that look alike are seen as one group

name: Closure, continuity & contiguity
q: What are the Gestalt principles of closure, continuity and contiguity?
ans:
Closure: completing figures that are incomplete
Continuity: seeing things as simply as possible, as a continuous pattern rather than broken up
Contiguity: two things that happen close together in time are seen as related

name: Depth perception: monocular vs binocular cues
q: What is depth perception, and how do monocular cues differ from binocular cues?
ans:
Depth perception: seeing the world in three dimensions
Monocular (pictorial) cues: work with one eye; artists use them to show depth
Binocular cues: need both eyes

name: Linear perspective, relative size & texture gradient
q: How do linear perspective, relative size and texture gradient signal distance?
ans:
Linear perspective: parallel lines appear to converge in the distance
Relative size: an object that looks smaller than expected is assumed to be farther away
Texture gradient: textured surfaces look smaller and finer as distance increases

name: Aerial perspective, overlap, motion parallax & accommodation
q: How do aerial perspective, overlap, motion parallax and accommodation signal distance?
ans:
Aerial perspective: farther objects look hazier, so seem more distant
Overlap (interposition): a blocked object is assumed to be behind and farther away
Motion parallax: close objects seem to move faster than far ones
Accommodation: the brain uses changes in lens thickness to judge distance

name: Convergence vs binocular disparity
q: How do the binocular cues of convergence and binocular disparity work?
ans:
Convergence: both eyes rotate to focus on one object; more for close objects, less for far ones (a muscular cue)
Binocular disparity: difference between the two eyes' images; bigger for close objects, smaller for distant ones

name: Perceptual illusions
q: What is a perceptual illusion? Explain the Müller-Lyer and moon illusions.
ans:
A perception that doesn't match reality
Müller-Lyer: inward- or outward-turning ends make equal lines look different lengths
Moon illusion: on the horizon, buildings in front make the moon look larger; in the sky there's nothing to compare
Rotating snakes and the Enigma: motion seen partly due to eye movements (microsaccades)
Hermann's grid: dots appear at the intersections

name: Perceptual set
q: What is a perceptual set (perceptual expectancy)?
ans:
Tendency to perceive things a certain way because of previous experiences or expectations
What you see depends on what you expect to see

name: Top-down vs bottom-up processing
q: How does top-down processing differ from bottom-up processing? Use the puzzle example.
ans:
Top-down: uses pre-existing knowledge to organise features into a whole (e.g. using the finished picture to do a puzzle)
Bottom-up: analyses small features to build a complete perception (e.g. doing a new puzzle without the picture)
Most of the time both are used together
